role.text: In view because this Story happens here.
On 6 May 1602 the city council asked the king to shut the trade with the Philippines.
The city's merchants had a guild of their own from 1594. The law kept them out of the Manila trade, and they traded all the same.
In 1598 a man asked the council for leave to open 'a Chinese shop' in the street of the cloth sellers.
A poem printed here in 1604 boasts of silk from China and of goods from Macao.
Antonio de Morga came here from Manila as a judge.
People brought across the Pacific and held as slaves worked in its households and its textile mills.
The map shows today's ground and draws no lake here. In these years the city stood on an island in a lake and was reached by causeways.
The marker shows present-day Mexico City; it is not a surveyed position for the city of 1602.

placeContext.headerLine: Jurisdiction not yet researched in this pilot

role.text: In view because the ships from Manila landed here.
Morga, who landed here on 19 December 1603, called it a good, sheltered port with a royal treasury, eighty leagues from Mexico City.
Duty and freight on the goods were taken here.
The ships for Manila left from here at the end of February or in March.
In 1602 or 1603 officials here held a woman named Gracia, whom the record calls a slave, because she had been sent without a licence.
No Source we have read describes the town or its people in 1602.
The marker shows present-day Acapulco, an approximate location.

entities.historicalName: The Manila trade in Mexico City

connection.directionNote: Manila to Acapulco by sea, then by road to Mexico City. Chinese goods one way, silver the other. Directional; not symmetric.
connection.directionFigureText: Manila  →  enabled  →  Mexico City, for silver

spatial.targetText: Mexico City · settlement precision · by way of Acapulco, the one port allowed
spatial.routeStatement: Each year the king's ships left the Philippines with Chinese silk and other goods and made Acapulco five or six months later. From there the goods went up to Mexico City by mule, and silver went back the same way. The law allowed two ships, goods worth 250,000 pesos, and trade by residents of the Philippines only. In 1603 the king himself wrote that these limits had been much exceeded. One man who made the crossing in 1603, Antonio de Morga, left an account of it. No Source we have read describes a cargo being landed, sold or carried up the road in 1602. The same ships carried people held as slaves, most of whom the port's books do not record.
spatial.accountsSentence: The same ships carried people held as slaves, most of whom the port's books do not record.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Woodrow Borah (1954) and Guillermina del Valle Pavón (2005) both describe this trade as Chinese goods for American silver, run in practice by the merchants of Mexico City in spite of the law. They rest on the same council minutes and viceroys' letters. How much silver it moved is not agreed: the king was told more than two million a year in 1603, and the city council said three million in 1602.

mechanismText.text: Chinese goods cost far less in New Spain than what the fleets brought from Spain, and silver bought more in Asia.
The crown allowed the trade within limits set in 1593, and only to residents of the Philippines.
The ships used one port in New Spain, Acapulco, where the king had a treasury and officers.
The crossing took five or six months; the ships left the Philippines from late June and went back from Acapulco in February or March.
Duty and freight were charged at Acapulco. Morga gives ten per cent; the accounts, by one historian's reading, show five.
From Acapulco the goods went to Mexico City by a mule road eighty leagues long.
Mexico City's merchants, who had a guild of their own from 1594, shipped in others' names and kept partners in Manila. Officials at the ports, one historian writes, declined to open the boxes.
Part of what landed went on to Peru, which the law forbade.
The king's viceroys told him the limits could not be enforced.
How much silver went back is not known. The city council said three million a year in 1602, in a plea to have the trade shut.
This is how Manila came to supply Mexico City. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. The king and the Cardinal wrote from Spain; only Morga saw both ends.

participants.text: Merchants of Mexico City, who were barred from the trade and ran much of it
Their partners and agents at Manila
Residents of the Philippines, for whom the law reserved the trade, and who complained they were crowded out
The king's officers at Acapulco, who took duty and freight
The viceroys in Mexico City, who told the crown the limits could not be kept
The city council of Mexico City, which asked in 1602 for the trade to be shut
Buyers from Peru, who came to New Spain with silver
The merchants of Seville, who wanted the trade closed
Chinese merchants at Manila, who sold the goods and are named by no Source in this set
Tailors and shopkeepers of Mexico City, who ordered and sold Chinese silk
Silk raisers of Puebla, whose trade fell
People carried east and held as slaves, among them a woman named Gracia, detained at Acapulco in 1602 or 1603

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: One eyewitness of the route, Morga, an official writing six years after his crossing. The king's letter repeats what his viceroys wrote; the Cardinal's repeats what Seville's traders told him. The council's letter is a plea, and its figures are its own. The two modern historians both work from the council's minutes and the viceroys' letters, and one of them misreported the council's figure. No Chinese Source, no Indigenous Source and no merchant's own account book is among them.

reverseDisclosure.body: Silver from Mexico City to Manila is the other half of this trade. The Manila 1602 Story follows it from there to the ships from China. What the silver's loss did inside New Spain, and where it was mined, are different Connections with their own Sources. They are not researched here.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one.

jurisdictionLine.text: In 1602 Mexico City had a viceroy, a city council and a merchant guild, each of which speaks in this Story. Acapulco had a chief magistrate and a royal treasury, by Morga's account. Which jurisdiction each place lay in has not been researched, so none is shown and no boundary is drawn.

body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Mexico City in 1602: the Chinese goods that reached it from Manila each year, and the one Connection this pilot explains for it, Manila to Mexico City by way of Acapulco. Acapulco, the port, is drawn to the south-west. One part of the Story is about the people who were carried on the same ships, held as slaves.

segments.text: What Morga saw when he landed. His book gives the day and nothing more.
What the silk raisers and weavers of New Spain said. None speaks in any Source we have read.
What Indigenous residents of the city bought or wore, in their own words.
Who carried the goods up the road, and what a cargo was in 1602.
What duty was really paid at Acapulco. Morga gives ten per cent; one historian finds five in the accounts.
How many people were carried, in any year. The port's books record a few; an official in Mexico City counted far more.
Where Gracia came from, and what became of her. We know her by one name, from a record about who owned her.
What any of them said in words of their own. Moreno's account reaches us through a petition, in a historian's English.
How much of the trade Mexico City's merchants ran. One historian's reading of one account book is what we have.
How much silver left Acapulco in a year. The council said three million and the king was told more than two; neither is a count.
What the viceroys wrote in their own words. We have a historian's report of it.
